claims.text: The report is 'AFSWC-TR-59-39, TR 59-39 Vol I, A STUDY OF LUNAR RESEARCH FLIGHTS', issued by 'HEADQUARTERS AIR FORCE SPECIAL WEAPONS CENTER, AIR RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT COMMAND, KIRTLAND AIR FORCE BASE, NEW MEXICO', authored by L. Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation, Illinois Institute of Technology, dated 19 June 1959, under Project Number 5776-57853 and Contract AF 29(601)-1164. Its title page marks the title '(Unclassified Title)'. The string 'A119' appears nowhere in the report.

The abstract opens: 'Nuclear detonations in the vicinity of the moon are considered in this report along with scientific information which might be obtained from such explosions. The military aspect is aided by investigation of space environment, detection of nuclear device testing, and capability of weapons in space.'

claims.source: AFSWC TR-59-39 Vol I, Chapter I, Introduction, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_AD0425380/DTIC_AD0425380_djvu.txt
claims.text: The introduction states the political motive in the report's own words: 'The motivation for such a detonation is clearly threefold: scientific, military and political... Obviously, however, specific positive effects would accrue to the nation first performing such a feat as a demonstration of advanced technological capability. It is also certain that, unless the climate of world opinion were well-prepared in advance, a considerable negative reaction could be stimulated.'

desc: A contractor study for the Air Force Special Weapons Center on what could be learned from detonating a nuclear weapon on or near the Moon, and on what it would cost politically. Its own introduction names three motivations, scientific, military and political, and says plainly that a nation performing the feat first would accrue positive effects as a demonstration of advanced technological capability. It is carried on this board as an instrument rather than an anecdote: a dated federal record of a plan whose public existence was, for decades, a matter of assertion. Its distribution list also documents who in the nuclear weapons complex received it. Two corrections the record forces on the corpus: the report is dated 19 June 1959, not 1958 and not May 1959, and the string A119 appears nowhere in it. C. E. Sagan is on its contributor list; the document says nothing about his security clearance.

dossier.denialPosture: No denial attaches to this document on this board, and the popular framing that one should is the thing the record refuses. The claim usually made about it, that its existence was maintained as non-existent for four decades before a forced declassification, is not gradeable from the copy read: the DDC copy carries UNCLASSIFIED markings, an expressly unclassified title, and no declassification stamp, downgrading instruction or distribution limitation anywhere in the OCR. That is not a finding that the study was never withheld. It is a finding that this board holds no document establishing that it was, which is a different sentence and the only one the record supports.
dossier.narrative:
The document says the political part out loud. Chapter I: 'The motivation for such a detonation is clearly threefold: scientific, military and political... Obviously, however, specific positive effects would accrue to the nation first performing such a feat as a demonstration of advanced technological capability. It is also certain that, unless the climate of world opinion were well-prepared in advance, a considerable negative reaction could be stimulated.' The abstract is narrower and more technical, offering space environment investigation, detection of nuclear device testing and weapons capability in space as the military aspect.

Three corrections this node forces on the wider corpus are the reason it is worth having. The string 'A119' appears nowhere in the report; the document identifies itself only by report number and contract. The date is 19 June 1959, not 1958 and not May 1959. And the claim that the study was denied and then declassified after four decades of maintained non-existence is not established by the copy read here: it carries UNCLASSIFIED markings on its cover pages, its title is expressly marked '(Unclassified Title)', and no declassification stamp, downgrading instruction or distribution limitation appears in the OCR. Whatever the classification history was, this copy does not carry it.

The Sagan question is answered only as far as the paper goes. C. E. Sagan is on the contributor list on the report page, and the appendix separately places C. Sagan on the National Academy of Sciences WESTEX group and on the Armed Forces National Research Council Panel on Extraterrestrial Life. The document says nothing whatever about his security clearance, and the fellowship-application story that usually travels with this report concerns a different document that has not been opened here.
openQuestions: The classification history of the study is not established. The DDC copy read here carries no declassification stamp or downgrading instruction, so whether an earlier copy was classified, and at what level, is unknown from this board.
The record here is Volume I. The board holds nothing on any further volume and has not established whether one exists.
The 1959 fellowship application in which the work is said to have been disclosed has not been opened. Nothing about it is in this report and no claim on this board rests on it.
Whether the copies sent to Sandia, Los Alamos, Lawrence Radiation Laboratory, ARPA and WADD survive in those institutions' records has not been tested by any request logged here.
dossier.whatItIs: AFSWC-TR-59-39, TR 59-39 Vol I, A Study of Lunar Research Flights, dated 19 June 1959 and issued by Headquarters Air Force Special Weapons Center, Air Research and Development Command, Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico. It was written by L. Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation at the Illinois Institute of Technology under Project Number 5776-57853 and Contract AF 29(601)-1164, with contributions from eleven others including C. E. Sagan. The copy read for this board is the Defense Documentation Center copy, AD 425380, read in full from the OCR text of the DTIC mirror.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is carried here as an instrument rather than as an anecdote. A dated federal record shows an Air Force laboratory paying a university research foundation to work out what could be learned from detonating a nuclear weapon on or near the Moon, and saying in its own introduction that one of the three motivations was political demonstration. The distribution list is the part with the most value to this board: it documents who in the nuclear weapons complex received a copy, which makes the report a custody record as well as a research study. Copies went to ARPA at the Pentagon, to the Atomic Energy Commission's technical reports library for the Division of Military Application, to Sandia Corporation's document control division, to Los Alamos, to Lawrence Radiation Laboratory and to WADD at Wright-Patterson.
